text: The historical view in the social sciences has always been that judgments are based solely on content information, with individuals being assumed to form judgments by systematically evaluating all available content information in an unbiased manner. However, over the past three decades, a considerable amount of research has challenged this assumption by showing that judgments may be formed not only on the basis of content information (cognitive judgments) but also on the basis of feelings (affective judgment). It is now well accepted that judgment can be both affective and cognitive. Whether it is one or the other depends on a multitude of factors: (1) the salience of the affective feelings, (2) the representativeness of the affective feelings for the target, (3) the relevance of the feelings for the judgment, (4) the evaluative malleability of the judgment, and (5) the level of processing intensity. | will discuss these in turn, and ultimately argue that generally speaking, in day-to- day life, the circumstances are generally those that result in affective rather than cognitive judgments and decision-making.
